newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil telecom bill allows Telebras break-up, sale.
newsitem.headline: Brazil telecom bill allows Telebras break-up, sale.

text.p: A bill creating Brazil's new telecommunications law authorizes the restructuring and sale of the federal Telebras SA system and creates a watchdog agency under the control of the Communications Ministry.
A copy of the bill listed Telebras's holding long-distance unit Embratel and 27 local subsidiaires as eligible to be merged and privatized.
The proposed law was delivered to Congress' lower house Thursday morning by Communications Minister Sergio Motta.
The bill outlines the creation of a regulatory body, which would be linked to the Communications Ministry and whose five members would be appointed by the president.

The watchdog, which would be called the Brazilian Telecommunications Agency, would set rates, award concessions and recommend government policy in the telecommunications sector. According to the bill, shareholders or groups of shareholders would be barred from controlling more than one concession.
Regarding the break-up and sell-off of Telebras, the bill also permits the federally owned firm's subsidiaries to be broken off into fixed and cellular units.
It also bars operators from merging conventional line services with companies providing cellular services.
The bill sets out the following additional points:
* The presidency will draft rules governing the regulatory body.
* The watchdog will act as an administrative authority, linked to the government but independent of firms providing telecoms services.
* The agency will determine who is granted telecoms concessions and will have power to extinguish them.
* The body will fix, control and monitor tariffs and ban cross subsidies.
* The agency will be run by a five-member directing council whose members will sit for five years, with the possibility of a second term.
* The regulator's first members will have mandates of between three and seven years in order to stagger their replacement.
* The law would bar any practices deemed to go against against free-market principles or competition, including subsidies to artificially lower rates.
* The law would allow the presidency to restructure the 29 units of the federal Telebras system, which may be broken up, merged or sold.
* The bill sets a maximum 20-year term for telecom operating concessions, which may be renewed for a further maximum 20-year period.
* Concession fees must be paid in cash but the payment may be made in installments.
* Groups seeking pre-qualification to bid for concessions will be required to show their technical and financial ability and show experience operating telecoms.
* Concessions will only be granted to firms based in Brazil which observe Brazilian corporate law.
* Control of a concession may only be sold five years after it is initially granted.
* Control of concessions after that five-year period may not be sold to an existing concessionnaire unless the agency should revoke in the future the one group-one concession rule.
* Within 60 days of the law's approval, existing fixed-line operators must ask for concessions for their service areas, which would go into effect within 24 months.
* Concessions for the existing firms would be free, last until December 31, 2005 and be renewable for 20 years.
* Cellular concessions will be awarded according to the terms of a law passed earlier this year.
* Five years after the signing of a concession, the regulating agency may allow a concession holder the freedom to set its own tariffs.
* The body could recover its tariff-setting powers if it felt increases were unjustified.
The bill, which has been anxiously awaited by the telecomms industry, is now due to begin committee-level study in the Chamber of Duputies.
Lawmakers have said the proposed law will be placed on the agenda for a special session of Congress set to begin on Janaury 6.
-- William Schomberg, Brasilia newsroom 5561 223 0358
